newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU leaders see careers hanging on single currency.
newsitem.headline: EU leaders see careers hanging on single currency.

text.p: Europe's political leaders are increasingly finding their careers tied to the success or failure of monetary union, with a number facing exile to the political wilderness if events turn against them.

Nowhere is this more evident than in Britain where Prime Minister John Major and his ruling Conservatives look likely to be thrown out of office on Thursday partly due to their inability to present a united front on the single currency.

But across the European Union, from Sweden to Spain, government and opposition leaders are hanging their reputations on economic and monetary union (EMU) -- and facing the wrath of voters if things go wrong.

German Chancellor Helmut Kohl has launched another run at reelection in order to ensure EMU gets past a sceptical public. French President Jacques Chirac has gambled on early assembly elections partly to guarantee his country makes the cut.
Chirac wants the freedom to take the budgetary steps necessary to meet EMU's strict deficit rules.

The stakes are high. If victory goes to the opposition Socialists, who have begun making sceptical noises about EMU, Chirac will find himself sharing power and struggling to recover from an electoral snub.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi has been the most open in linking his future to the single currency, due to be adopted in qualifying countries on January 1, 1999.
He has promised on a number of occasions, most recently last week, that he will resign if Italy does not make it in the first wave of countries to adopt the euro.
His struggle is not against public opinion, which firmly supports monetary union, but against Germany and other hardline EU countries which fear the Italian economy is not ready for EMU.
By contrast, Swedish Prime Minister Goran Persson has the economy to qualify for the euro and would like to see his country adopt it.

But opposition within his Social Democrat party as well as from the Swedish public and the Centre Party with which he has an informal alliance, threatens his hold on government should he push for EMU.
A general election there next year looks set to be fought on European issues with EMU heading the list.

Further south, in Madrid and Lisbon, politicans are less vulnerable to EMU scepticism. But they have geared their economic policies so much to being in the first wave of EMU countries that failure could be a severe blow at least to their pride.
As in other countries, it could also be much harder to push through further, sometimes painful, budget cuts needed to qualify in a second wave.
Spanish Prime Minister Jose-Maria Aznar, leading a minority government, could find it particularly humbling if his country does not qualify for the first wave and neighbouring, tiny, Portugal does.
Elsewhere political leaders who support EMU, including Kohl, are in danger of clashing directly with their voters.
Danish Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen, for example, supports Denmark's long-term participation in EMU despite the fact that his country has already rejected it in a referendum.
In Austria, both ruling coalition partners, the centre-left Social Democrats and the conservative People's Party, back EMU, while polls show that about half the nation does not.
